title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems
authors: Ian Baum, Riley B. Dawkins, Jannatul Ferdous, Omar S. Magana-Loaiza
abstract: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.
summary: This paper reports the first experimental measurement of the quantum phase in multiparticle photonic systems containing up to fifteen particles. By combining homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection, the authors established the number-phase uncertainty relation. This work provides a vital operational tool for characterizing quantum phase in complex quantum optical systems.
main_problem: The quantum phase of multiparticle systems is poorly understood due to the lack of a suitable phase operator, preventing the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number.
main_result: The authors successfully measured the quantum phase of up to fifteen-particle photonic systems, establishing the number-phase uncertainty relation and providing an operational framework for phase measurement.
method: They employed a novel quantum state tomography scheme combining homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations.
model_or_system: The study focuses on multiparticle photonic systems, analyzing the quantum state density matrix ($\hat{ho}$) in both the Fock (number) and phase bases.
key_observables: Quantum phase ($\phi$), photon number ($n$), and the derived trigonometric observables ($\hat{C}$ and $\hat{S}$) used to characterize phase.
important_parameters: Up to fifteen particles; the number-phase uncertainty relation ($\Delta n \Delta \phi \geq \dots$).
main_assumptions: The necessity of constructing Hermitian trigonometric observables ($\hat{C}, \hat{S}$) because the initial phase operator ($\hat{E}$) is not Hermitian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup for spatially-resolved tomography combining homodyne interferometry and PNR detection, and show the number-phase Fourier duality in spatially resolved fields.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework for phase operators ($\hat{E}, \hat{C}, \hat{S}$), details the measurement technique (homodyne/PNR tomography), derives the number-phase uncertainty relation, and finally applies this framework to measure and map the phase in multiparticle systems.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial experimental methodology for characterizing quantum phase in complex photonic systems, which is fundamental for understanding quantum correlations and developing quantum information protocols.

The periodic nature of quantum phase prevents its direct characterization through a linear average of phase values. The trigonometric observables ˆC and ˆS circumvent this ambiguity by providing a representation that preserves the periodicity of phase. FIG. 3. Number–phase Fourier duality in spatially resolved multiphoton fields. Our spatially resolved quantum state tomography reveals the complementary photon-number and phase structure of a multiphoton field. As shown in a, we demonstrate the possibility of distilling the constituent multiphoton subsystems of a classical light field from its mean photon-number (intensity) distribution. This capability is illustrated for n = 0, 1, and 5, revealing distinct spatial distributions for each multiphoton subsystem. The complementary phase representation is shown in b, where the reconstructed quantum phase is resolved into multiphoton phase subsystems with well-defined values ϕ = 0, π/4, and π/2....

FIG. 4. Mapping the number–phase uncertainty of a multiphoton field. Our spatially resolved quantum state tomography enables the direct experimental characterization of the number–phase uncertainty product, ∆n∆ϕ, across a co- herent multiphoton field. The measured uncertainty exhibits a pronounced spatial dependence, approaching the lower bound in regions of low photon number and increasing toward the center of the field. The photon-number and phase distribu- tions at representative positions a–c reveal the complementary fluctuations underlying this behavior.
